Fourteenth
fôr'tēnth
a. (the ordinal of fourteen; in the Law, the fixed day of the Passover)
From fourteen with the ordinal ending -th. In Hebrew the ordinal above ten is simply the cardinal used ordinally, arbaah asar, four and ten.

Biblical Definition

Fourteenth is one of the most legally fixed words in the Old Testament, because it names the day on which the Passover lamb dies. The lamb is taken on the tenth of the first month and kept up “until the fourteenth day of the same month: and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening” (Exo 12:6). Leviticus repeats it as statute: “In the fourteenth day of the first month at even is the LORD'S passover” (Lev 23:5). The date does not float. It survives the wilderness, the conquest, the divided kingdom, Hezekiah's and Josiah's reformations, and the return from exile; and it is the day on which the Lord Jesus is crucified, so that the antitype falls on the calendar the type had held for fifteen centuries. Paul draws the conclusion without argument: “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” (1Co 5:7). The fourteenth is God's appointment, kept by God, in the death of God's Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives fourteenth as the ordinal of fourteen, the fourth after the tenth, and notes the fourteenth day of the first month as the day of the Jewish passover.

expand to see more

FOURTEENTH, a. The ordinal of fourteen; the fourth after the tenth.

2. Making one of fourteen equal parts into which a whole is divided.

Note. The passover was killed on the fourteenth day of the first month, at even. Exod. xii. 6; Lev. xxiii. 5.

Note. The second passover, for such as were unclean, was kept on the fourteenth day of the second month. Num. ix. 11.

Key Scripture

Exo 12:6 — "And ye shall keep it up until the fourteenth day of the same month: and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening."

Lev 23:5 — "In the fourteenth day of the first month at even is the LORD'S passover."

Gen 7:20 — "Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered."

Gal 1:18 — "Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days."

Modern Corruption

The fixed date is dissolved into a general theme of liberation, so that the Passover becomes a symbol of freedom in the abstract rather than an appointed sacrifice on an appointed day.

expand to see more

Liberation-theology treatments of the Exodus habitually retain the deliverance and discard the lamb. But Exo 12 puts the blood before the departure: Israel is not freed and then given a ritual to remember it by; Israel is spared on the fourteenth because a substitute died in the house, and the going out follows. Strip the date and the lamb, and what remains is a political parable that could be told about any oppressed people, which is precisely why the framework finds it useful and precisely why it is not what Moses wrote.

The exactness of the fourteenth also answers a subtler corruption: the notion that typology is a devotional overlay the church invented after the fact. A statute given in Egypt, repeated in Leviticus, and kept for centuries fixed the calendar square on which the crucifixion would fall. Neither Israel nor the Sanhedrin arranged that. It is the plainest available evidence that the Old Testament's furniture was built to a plan, and that the plan was the cross.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arbaah asar (H702 with H6240), four and ten, used ordinally for the fourteenth day; Greek tessareskaidekatos (G5065), fourteenth.

expand to see more

Hebrew arbaah asar — “four ten”; Hebrew uses the cardinal for ordinals above ten, so the fourteenth day is simply the day “four and ten”.

Hebrew pesach (H6453) — passover, from pasach, to pass or leap over; the feast named for what the LORD did on that night.

Hebrew ben haarbayim — “between the evenings”, the KJV's “in the evening” of Exo 12:6, the interval in which the lamb is killed.

Greek tessareskaidekatos (G5065) — fourteenth; used by Luke of the day of the shipwreck watch (Act 27:27, 33).

Num 9:11 — the second passover, for the unclean and the traveller, on the fourteenth of the second month; the day is moved but never the date within the month.

Usage

"“Until the fourteenth day of the same month” — the lamb kept four days, then killed."

"“In the fourteenth day… is the LORD'S passover” — a statute, not a custom."

"The fourteenth of Abib — the calendar square on which type and antitype meet."
